intro.html: Three Greek parts build all ten words in this topic. path means feeling (or suffering), phil means love, and anthrop means human being. Add a prefix or a second part and you can read the word like a tiny sentence: phil + anthrop is “loves people,” and mis + anthrop is “hates people.”

path = feeling: apathy (a- = without: no feeling), empathy (em- = in: feeling with someone), antipathy (anti- = against: a feeling against), pathos (what stirs feeling), telepathy (tele- = far: feeling across a distance). phil = love: philanthropist, bibliophile. anthrop = human: philanthropist, misanthrope, anthropology, anthropomorphic.
Once you know these parts you can guess dozens of other words: sympathy, philosophy (love of wisdom), philharmonic (love of harmony), anthropoid (humanlike).

words.def: lack of interest, feeling or concern
words.ex: The team’s {apathy} was plain: no one even came to the last practice.
words.ctx: The club failed not because anyone opposed it but because of {apathy}; hardly anyone cared enough to come to meetings or to vote.
words.etym: From Greek apatheia, “freedom from feeling”: a- (without) + pathos (feeling).

mn.text: The class garden is wilting in the sun, but everyone just shrugs and walks past: nobody cares. That is {apathy}.

scene.alt: Two bored teens shrug and walk past drooping flowers that no one waters.

words.def: the ability to understand and share another person’s feelings
words.ex: Thanks to his {empathy}, Sami always knew when a friend needed cheering up.
words.ctx: Instead of laughing when Kai dropped his lunch tray, Rosa showed {empathy}: she remembered how embarrassed she had felt last year and quietly helped him clean up.
words.etym: From Greek em- (in) + pathos (feeling); English took the word up in the early 1900s.

mn.text: When Dev’s kite breaks, Lila feels his sadness as if it were her own and gives him a hug: she has {empathy}.

scene.alt: A girl hugs a crying boy whose kite lies broken on the grass.

words.ex: Grandpa’s {antipathy} toward loud music was no secret.
words.ctx: Their {antipathy} began with a quarrel over a fence, and for twenty years the two neighbors refused even to say good morning to each other.

mn.text: From the day they met, Whiskers the cat and Rufus the dog have glared and growled at each other: they share a deep {antipathy}.

scene.alt: A cat and a dog glare and growl at each other.

words.def: a quality in a story, speech or scene that stirs pity or sadness
words.ex: The movie’s last scene, with the old dog waiting by the door, is full of {pathos}.
words.ctx: The speech was not clever or funny, but its {pathos} moved everyone; by the end, many listeners were quietly wiping their eyes.

mn.text: In the school play, the lost puppy walks its lonely path home through the rain, and the audience reaches for tissues: the scene is full of {pathos}.

scene.alt: On a stage, a sad puppy walks under a rain cloud while audience members cry.

words.def: the supposed sending of thoughts from one mind to another without words
words.ex: The twins joked that they had {telepathy} because they always ordered the same sandwich.
words.ctx: In the science-fiction novel, the two pilots talk by {telepathy}, sending thoughts silently across hundreds of miles without any radio.
words.etym: Made up in English in the 1880s from Greek tele (far) + pathos (feeling).
words.note: Telepathy is common in stories; there is no scientific evidence that it is real.

mn.text: Zoe is at one end of the town and Kai at the other, yet both suddenly think “Pizza!” at the same moment: they joke that it is {telepathy}.

scene.alt: Two children far apart think of the same pizza at the same moment.

words.def: a person who gives money or time to help others
words.ex: A local {philanthropist} paid for new books in every classroom.
words.ctx: Though she had grown rich selling furniture, the {philanthropist} lived simply and gave most of her money to hospitals and schools.
words.etym: From Greek philanthropos, “loving people”: philein (to love) + anthropos (human being).

mn.cue: PHIL loves ANTHROPOS: Phil loves people
mn.text: Phil loves people so much that he pays for a brand-new park where everyone in town can play: Phil is a {philanthropist}.

scene.alt: Children cheer a smiling man named Phil under a banner thanking him for a new playground.

words.ex: The {bibliophile} had books stacked on every chair in his house.
words.ctx: A true {bibliophile}, Granny Mae could not walk past a bookstore without going in, and she owned three copies of her favorite novel.
words.etym: From French bibliophile, from Greek biblion (book) + philos (loving).

mn.text: Granny Mae hugs her newest book like an old friend, surrounded by towers of the ones she already loves: she is a {bibliophile}.

scene.alt: A grandmother hugs a book lovingly, surrounded by stacks of books.

words.def: a person who dislikes people in general
words.ex: The grumpy {misanthrope} in the story lives alone on a cliff and turns away every visitor.
words.ctx: Though the old writer was called a {misanthrope} because he avoided parties and crowds, his letters show that he deeply loved a few close friends.
words.etym: From Greek misanthropos, “hating people”: misein (to hate) + anthropos (human being).

mn.text: Rex lives alone at the top of the hill behind a sign that says GO AWAY, and he grumbles at every friendly visitor: he is a {misanthrope}.

scene.alt: A friendly neighbor waves with a pie, but a grump by his house and a GO AWAY sign just grumbles.

words.def: the study of human beings and their ways of life
words.ex: Maya plans to study {anthropology} to learn how people around the world celebrate the new year.
words.ctx: Her work in {anthropology} took her to dozens of villages, where she recorded how families farmed, cooked, told stories and raised their children.

mn.cue: ANTHROPO + LOGY: the study of PEOPLE
mn.text: Ada spends a year in a mountain village, writing down how people cook, dance, farm and tell stories: she works in {anthropology}.

scene.alt: A woman takes notes as villagers dance and clap at a festival.

words.def: giving human form or traits to animals or things
words.ex: Fairy tales are full of {anthropomorphic} animals who talk and wear clothes.
words.ctx: The cartoon gave the toaster {anthropomorphic} features, a smiling face and waving arms, so that it seemed like a cheerful friend.
words.etym: From Greek anthropomorphos, “shaped like a human”: anthropos (human being) + morphe (form).

mn.text: In Lila’s picture book, the cat sits at the breakfast table, sips tea and says “Good morning!” just like a person: the cat is {anthropomorphic}.

scene.alt: A cat sits at the breakfast table with a cup of tea, saying good morning like a person.

after.cap: Read the parts and the word explains itself.

after.html: empathy is feeling with someone, as if you were in their place. sympathy is feeling sorry for someone. You can sympathize with a friend whose team lost without sharing the feeling; empathy means you feel the loss too.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The voters’ {apathy} was clear: only one person in ten showed up.

after.cap: Not caring at all is apathy; antipathy is a strong dislike.

items.q: The two rival chefs could not stand each other. Between them there was…
items.why: Antipathy (anti, against + path, feeling) is a strong dislike. Apathy means not caring at all.

items.q: Lila feels her friend’s nervousness before the recital almost as if it were her own. Lila has…
items.why: Empathy is sharing another person’s feelings, feeling with them.

items.q: True or false: a misanthrope and a philanthropist are near opposites.
items.why: True. Both contain anthrop (human being), but mis- means hate and phil means love.

items.q: Use the parts: bibli = book, phil = love, anthrop = human, logy = study. Type the word that means “the study of human beings.”
